summary: Describes privacy partitioning, which spreads data and communication across multiple parties so that identity is separate from user data. It describes emerging protocol patterns, gives terminology, and discusses how to analyze such designs.

plainLanguage.summary: If one person knows your name and another knows what you bought, neither learns everything. This explains designing systems that way.

questions: how can i separate my identity from my data online
subtitle: Spreading data across parties to protect identity while preserving function.

tldr.problem: When a user sends data to a service, the service sees both who the user is (their identity) and what they do (their data). Combining these reveals too much: a bank knows an account holder's transactions; a search engine knows a user's queries and IP address; a content server knows what you read and who you are.
tldr.mechanism: Privacy partitioning intentionally splits data and communication across multiple independent entities so that no single party (except the user) sees both identity and data. For example, a relay sees the user's IP but not their request; a gateway sees the request but not the IP. Encryption and separate connections enforce these boundaries.
tldr.outcome: When correctly applied, partitioning makes it technically harder for services or attackers to correlate user identity with user behavior. The principle is now used in protocols like Oblivious HTTP, Privacy Pass, and MASQUE proxying. However, partitioning works only if the parties do not collude and if all layers of the system follow the principle.

facts.label: Protocols discussed
facts.value: MASQUE, Oblivious HTTP, Privacy Pass, DAP

today: RFC 9614 is an IAB Informational RFC. Privacy partitioning is an emerging architectural pattern now used in multiple IETF working groups (OHAI, MASQUE, Privacy Pass, PPM). The principle is not new but the document provides unified terminology and analysis. Deployments increasingly use partitioning techniques for privacy-sensitive applications, though operational challenges (such as anti-abuse without IP data) remain open.

sections.title: The Problem: Identity Plus Data
sections.content:
Secure channels between a user and a service (like HTTPS) protect data in transit but do not protect privacy. A service that encrypts data still sees your IP address, your account name, your request timing, and the content itself. The service can link these together: it knows that a specific user account accessed specific resources at specific times.

This linkage of user identity (who) with user data (what) is the core privacy problem. A news service learns who reads what. A health app learns what a person searches for. A merchant learns what a person buys. Privacy partitioning aims to prevent any single service from seeing both.

The principle is simple: keep identity and data separate by ensuring different parties see each piece. It is an application of the principle of least privilege: give each party only the minimum information they need.
sections.plainLanguage: A regular online store sees who you are and what you buy. A privacy-partitioned system splits this: one party checks who you are, another processes your purchase without knowing your name. The two parties do not talk to each other, so nobody knows your full story.

sections.title: Privacy Contexts and Separation
sections.content:
A privacy context is a set of data, metadata, and the entities that share access to that information. When a user interacts with a service over HTTPS, there is one context containing the user's data and the service's identity. To partition this, the user must create separate contexts using two techniques:

Encryption limits which parties can see which data. A relay that sees encrypted data cannot read it; only parties with the decryption key can. Connection separation creates physical or logical boundaries: a user might use one connection to a relay and a separate connection through that relay to a target, so the relay never sees the direct connection to the target.

Combining these techniques creates multiple overlapping contexts. A user connecting through two proxies creates separate contexts between (1) user and proxy A, (2) proxy A and proxy B, and (3) proxy B and target. Each hop sees only the traffic passing through it, not the end-to-end content.
sections.plainLanguage: A context is a view of what is happening: what data is visible and to whom. When you add encryption or proxy through an intermediary, you split the view so different parties see different pieces. You want each party to see only the parts they need.

sections.title: Protocols Using Partitioning
sections.content:
Several IETF protocols now use privacy partitioning. MASQUE (Multiplexed Application Substrate over QUIC Encryption) uses forward proxies with encryption: a client connects to a proxy over encrypted QUIC, then the proxy tunnels encrypted traffic to a target. The proxy sees the transport (which proxy is being used) but not the encrypted end-to-end content.

Oblivious HTTP uses per-message encryption with a relay and gateway. The relay sees that a client is accessing a particular gateway but cannot decrypt the message. The gateway decrypts and processes the message but cannot see the client's IP. No single party sees both.

Privacy Pass partitions issuance from redemption. In the issuance context, an attester and issuer interact with a client to verify and issue tokens. In the redemption context, the client uses tokens at an origin server without revealing who they are. These happen at different times and with different entities.

Privacy Preserving Measurement (DAP) splits client identity from individual measurements using secret sharing: measurement servers collectively compute aggregate statistics without learning individual values.
sections.plainLanguage: Oblivious HTTP: one server sees your IP, another server sees your question, but neither sees both. Privacy Pass: you prove you are human to one service, then use that proof at another service without saying who you are. MASQUE: you ask a proxy to connect to a target, and the proxy does not see what you do with the target.

sections.title: Applying Partitioning Correctly
sections.content:
To apply privacy partitioning, first identify what information is user-identifying (email, IP address, account names) and what is user data (the requests, the content). Then partition so that user-identifying information and user data are never visible to the same party except the client.

A critical step is choosing client identifiers. If a user logs into two different services with the same email address, even if network-level partitioning hides the IP, the email address can link the user across contexts. Better practice is to use unique identifiers per context (unique email per service, randomized MAC addresses, temporary IP addresses).

Partitioning can fail if it is incomplete. Encrypting the network layer but allowing the application layer to send the user account ID defeats the purpose. VPNs hide the destination but not the user's identity to the VPN server. Partitioning must be applied consistently across layers.
sections.plainLanguage: First, figure out what is private and what is identity. Then make sure different parties see each one. Do not use the same name at different services, or you link yourself across them. Make sure privacy works all the way down, not just at the network level.

sections.title: When Partitioning Fails
sections.content:
Privacy partitioning is not a complete solution. It fails when parties collude: if the relay and gateway in Oblivious HTTP work together, they can reconstruct which client sent which request just by matching timing of messages in and out.

It also fails with side channels. Even if a proxy cannot see encrypted data, it can observe the size and timing of packets, potentially inferring the encrypted content through traffic analysis. Similarly, partitioning at the network layer cannot prevent the application layer from leaking data: a telemetry system could embed the user's real name in the telemetry data itself, defeating IP-level partitioning.

A subtler failure is fingerprinting: device properties, browser behaviors, and other characteristics can make an otherwise anonymous client identifiable, linking partitioned contexts back to the same person.

Finally, partitioning imposes costs: more hops mean latency, anti-abuse systems must work without IP addresses, and centralization of proxies or relays can become a bottleneck. Properly evaluating a partitioning design requires holistic security analysis, not just cryptographic assessment.
sections.plainLanguage: If the two servers secretly share information, they can still figure out who you are. Even with encryption, watching packet sizes and timing can leak clues. If a website puts your name in the encrypted data, the proxy still learns it. And if you have a distinctive device, people can follow you across contexts anyway.
